reviews.review:
I first played through Mass Effect: Andromeda in 2019, and actually had some rather fond memories of it despite being wary of the negative public sentiment surrounding the game. It was also the first time I ever played a Mass Effect game. Without the baggage of the previous titles, when seeing the game for what it was, I thoroughly enjoyed the gameplay; it had some interesting puzzles, unique skill expression, and an intriguing world. However, I also recognised that the story was just serviceable, and left a lot to be desired.

A few years later, I finally got around to playing through the original trilogy through the Legendary Edition, albeit with mods that expanded content and graphics. While the actual gameplay was notably dated, the story blew me away. Seeing how choices propagated through the games was quite a feat, and something that I don't think has ever been replicated to the same extent. The character writing was also excellent. I was genuinely invested in all of the characters on the Normandy, even if I did have my favourites. The original trilogy is a work of art, and I had a much better understanding of why MEA was so poorly received at launch. It was burdened by the expectations built up by the games that came before, even though it was focused on a completely different story with different characters. After finishing the original trilogy, I knew I'd want to return to MEA again (and as of writing, I have yet to finish it on this playthrough, but I still remember what is to come in the story for the most part; I will update this review if my appraisal changes upon completion) just to see how my feelings would change. Do note that my current playthrough is not vanilla. I've installed a bunch of quality of life mods like faster doors, community fixes, and a less intrusive UI. I've also installed some cosmetic mods.

The first thing that stood out to me was the combat. I really enjoy what BioWare did with the sandbox. It basically took the strengths of ME3 combat, introduced more verticality and agility, and gave it a few more dimensions for personal customisation. However, I really wish squad control and customisation was not dumbed down. I miss changing the squad's equipment (note that armour equipping has been removed since ME2) and being able to chain the squad's skills together. In MEA, they serve more as cannon fodder to draw away enemy aggression, especially on Insanity difficulty. Despite the regressions, I still enjoy the gunplay in MEA more than that of the OT.

The open world was also a really interesting addition, albeit a little lacklustre. It is certainly much more engaging than the barren worlds of ME1 and gives a better sense of all these unique and expansive worlds that ME2/3 didn't quite capture with the more limited maps. However, it does also feel somewhat unfinished. You'll find yourself travelling for long stretches between key points with little to do in between aside from a couple of enemy encampments and a ridiculous amount of "additional tasks" which typically involve you interacting with or scanning something for a counter to go up. I think much of this can be attributed to the troubled development of MEA and how things didn't quite come together until ~2 years before release, which is a shame. The Nomad, quite like the Mako in ME1, is rather unwieldy. It feels good to drive until you inevitably spin out or hit a random rock that sends you flying in the opposite direction. In an odd and somewhat charming way, it makes traversal more engaging, but it also can be quite frustrating at times.

The story, as I mentioned, is just serviceable. Many of the themes seem like rehashes of the OT, which is disappointing since this was supposed to be a completely fresh start with brand new ideas to explore. It also feels like certain story beats should have been given greater emphasis. I recall the way we were introduced to the Citadel in ME1 and the way it fades in through the fog with a triumphant score; it was truly awe inspiring. But in MEA, you pull up to the Nexus to dock and it feels almost uneventful. There is a story reason behind this, but the reveal could have been delayed a little for what I feel would have been a more impactful twist. The way MEA presents its story and world really diminishes what few strengths it has. Many of the side quests also pale in comparison to what was present in previous titles, though some of them were still rather memorable. However, it is not all bad. I still enjoyed the character stories, even if some had clearly more planning than others, and I much prefer the new dialogue system over the arbitrary renegade/paragon system of the OT.

One "fault" I think people unjustly criticise MEA's story for, is the lack of consequences for your choices. Yes, individual side stories can have different conclusions based on your choices, but few of them pan out later in the story aside from the final battle, if at all. I think this is misguided, as we have to remember that MEA is still just one game. ME1 actually suffers from much of the same limitations; it was only in the later games when we truly started to see some of the lingering effects of our choices. I'm sure it was initially the plan to have MEA be part of a new trilogy of sorts, but was only scrapped after the poor reception on release. Sure, it can be argued that it should be better regardless, and I agree. But I also don't think we should write it off as bad when we unfairly compare it to the OT as a collection of games rather than each game as individual titles. Had a sequel to MEA been developed that furthered the Andromeda storyline, I have a feeling that MEA would retroactively become a little more positively received. It is unfortunate that that isn't the reality that we live in. Even more unfortunate is how it seems like the next Mass Effect game is similarly in development hell (let's hope for the best regardless).

Overall, I enjoyed my time with MEA back in 2019, and I still enjoy it on my current playthrough. It might rank as the lowest of all the Mass Effect games for me based on the circumstances, but I also think that says more about how good the OT was rather than the actual merit of MEA. It was definitely rushed out of the door; there's no denying the many flaws present. But it is still a good game that regularly goes on sale for less than $10. That's a perfectly reasonable price for what it brings to the table.

This is a game I would give a sideways to if I could. I gave it a thumbs up because once I did get into Andromeda it was alright. It took 7ish hours for me to finally click with it. I liked most of the crew (Jaal, my darling.) Story was decent, but it almost feels like they did a "you can copy my homework but change it up a bit." from the original trilogy. Biggest oof I had with the game was 1. Could not get my Ryder to look good, I just accepted defeat and 2. Combat wasn't that fun imho. Most other people like it, yet it never wowed me. Writing can be a little cringey at times, but I've heard way worse in other games. Decent enough game that bought during a sale is worth a shot.

7/10

Andromeda is a good game, but it's not a very good Mass Effect game. When compared to the original trilogy (even at their weakest), the flaws of this game become glaring. Instead of the focused, character-driven linear experience of the originals, Andromeda feels more like a MMO spinoff that's been unshelved and repackaged as the next big thing (it wasn't). Some of its worst offenses include lazy character design (dead eyes and copy-paste faces on Asaris), tedious one-dimensional side quests that have you fast travelling from point A to point B and then back to point A just to pad time, and finally, a lack of charm and depth that made the originals so special.

What the game does do well is combat and scenery. It's a beautiful game and when you're ripping through enemies, you feel the weight of every blow. Planets are incredibly well designed with gorgeous vistas and skies that truly make you feel like you're exploring an alien world for the first time. That said, this game did not deserve the 80+ hours I gave it since most of it was wasted on uninteresting dialogue with even less interesting characters, and I probably could have finished it in about half the time, but I will admit that throughout the 80+ hours were moments where I really thought "wow, this looks cool". The longer you spend playing this game, the more it starts to strain, so a 30-40 hour playthrough is more than enough for a pleasant experience.
